questiontext.text:
Goal

Write three short functions that print Python's three capitalised words, return the truth of a value, and branch on it.

How this works in Python

Java has one boolean type, spelled in lower case, and it is the only thing an if will take.

boolean armed = true;
String label = null;
if (armed) { ... }
if (count != 0) { ... }   // a number needs a comparison first

Python has a boolean type as well. It is called bool and it has two values, True and False, each written with a capital letter. Lower case true is not a Python word at all, and typing it raises NameError: name 'true' is not defined.

Python's stand-in for null is None, again with a capital letter. None is a real value. You can assign it, pass it, return it and print it, and printing one shows the word None.

armed = True
label = None
print(armed, label)      # True None

Then comes the part Java never prepared you for. An if in Python takes any value at all, not only a bool. Python asks the value whether it counts as true, and every value has an answer ready.

A value that counts as false is called falsey. Every other value is truthy. The falsey values you have met so far make a short list.

  • False itself.
  • None.
  • Zero, both the int 0 and the float 0.0.
  • The empty string "".
  • The empty list [].

Everything else is truthy. That includes the string "0", which is one character long, the list [0], which holds one item, and the single space " ". What matters is emptiness, never the contents.

So if count != 0: and if count: ask an integer the same question, and a Python programmer writes the second. To see the answer for yourself, call bool(value), which hands back a real True or False.

print(bool(""))     # False
print(bool("0"))    # True

In Java the compiler stops you from writing if (payload). Python allows it, and the harder tiers of this topic show you where that freedom bites. For now, learn to read it.

Your task

Write three short functions. No body here runs past four lines.

  • flags_and_gap() prints True, False and None on one line with single spaces between them. Use one call to print, hand it all three values, and let it place the spaces.
  • truth_of(value) returns the truth of value as a bool. One line, and bool does the work.
  • gate(value) prints go when value is truthy and stop when it is falsey. Test the value on its own, as if value:, with nothing after it.

You pass when each function prints or returns what it should and adds nothing else.

Rules
  • Compare against nothing. ==, !=, <, > and is are all banned.
  • Do not call len(). Emptiness is the question if already asks.
  • Write True, False and None with their capital letters. The lower case spellings do not exist.
  • Hand the work to bool in truth_of, on one line.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

No AI. Type every character yourself. This tier builds the muscle, and a tool that types it for you skips the exercise.

expected.text: True False None False True False True

testcode.text: print(truth_of([]), truth_of([0]), truth_of(None), truth_of(-3), truth_of(0.0)) gate(0) gate(" ") print("edge cases done")

expected.text: False True False True False stop go edge cases done

testcode.text: import ast, inspect answer = "".join(inspect.getsource(f) for f in (flags_and_gap, truth_of, gate)) tree = ast.parse(answer) assert not [n for n in ast.walk(tree) if isinstance(n, ast.Compare)], "rule broken: compare against nothing, test the value itself" assert not [n for n in ast.walk(tree) if isinstance(n, ast.Call) and getattr(n.func, "id", "") == "len"], "rule broken: no len()" assert "True" in answer and "False" in answer and "None" in answer, "rule broken: write the three words with their capital letters" assert "bool(" in inspect.getsource(truth_of), "rule broken: hand the work to bool()" print(truth_of(""), truth_of("x")) gate(0)

questiontext.text:
Goal

Write two functions and one report that tell an absent payload from an empty one and show what and and or hand back.

How this works in Python

In Java you check for absence one way and one way only.

if (payload != null) { ... }

That line has exactly one correct Python translation, and it is if payload is not None. It is never if payload.

Here is the reason. Python lets you put any value where a condition belongs, not only a boolean. A value that counts as false in a condition is called falsey. Every other value is truthy. The falsey list is longer than a Java developer expects. None is falsey. The int 0 and the float 0.0 are falsey. So are the empty string "", the empty list [], the empty dictionary {}, and every other empty container. A dictionary is Python's map from keys to values, written with curly braces, and an empty pair of braces makes an empty one.

Write the null check as a truth test and the legitimate empty case disappears. A payload of length zero arrives, your code decides that nothing arrived, and no exception is raised to tell anybody. Preventing that defect is why this exercise exists.

and and or hold the second surprise. Java's || produces a boolean. Python's or produces an operand, which means one of the two values you gave it. Python evaluates the left side first. If the left side is truthy, Python returns the left side. Otherwise Python returns the right side. So "" or "fallback" is the string "fallback" and not True. That behaviour turns or into a way of supplying a default value. and works as the mirror image and returns the first falsey operand, so 0 and 99 is 0.

Python also has a conditional expression. It is an expression rather than a statement, so it produces a value and you can return it directly. The value comes first and the test comes second.

result = "yes" if flag else "no"

Java's flag ? "yes" : "no" is the same idea with the three parts in a different order. To handle three outcomes, put a second conditional expression after the else.

Your task

Write two functions and one report.

  • status(payload) returns "MISSING" when payload is None, "EMPTY" when payload is falsey, and "OK" otherwise. Test for None first, because None is falsey too and the two answers differ. 0 and "" give "EMPTY" because they are falsey. [0] and "0" give "OK", because a container that holds something is truthy whatever it holds.
  • label(reading, fallback) returns reading when reading is truthy and returns fallback when it is not. One or does the whole job.
  • operand_report() prints the value that "" or "fallback" produces and the value that 0 and 99 produces, each one beside the name of its type. Print these two lines exactly.
'fallback' is a str
0 is a int

Write the value with {value!r}, the !r form from the strings and f-strings topic, so the string keeps its quotes. Write the type name with {type(value).__name__}. type(value) hands back the type itself, the way Java's getClass() does, and __name__ holds that type's name as a string.

You pass when the printed output matches the expected text exactly.

Rules
  • Write is None once. Nothing else in your answer may mention None. == None and != None are banned.
  • Do not call len(), and do not compare against 0, "" or [].
  • Write no if statement. Use a conditional expression or or.
  • Return on every path. Falling off the end returns None and the grader prints it.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

AI for explanation only. Ask it what an error means or why one form is more idiomatic. Do not let it write your answer.

expected.text: None -> MISSING [] -> EMPTY [0] -> OK '' -> EMPTY '0' -> OK 0 -> EMPTY
14.2 n/a -1 n/a 'fallback' is a str 0 is a int

testcode.text: print(status({}), status({"a": 1}), status(0.0), status(False)) print(label([], ["default"]), label({"k": 1}, {}))

import ast, inspect answer = "".join(inspect.getsource(f) for f in (status, label, operand_report)) assert answer.count("None") == 1, "rule broken: mention None exactly once" assert "== None" not in answer and "!= None" not in answer, "rule broken: no equality against None" for fn in (status, label): tree = ast.parse(inspect.getsource(fn)) assert not [n for n in ast.walk(tree) if isinstance(n, ast.If)], "rule broken: no if statement" assert not [n for n in ast.walk(tree) if isinstance(n, ast.Call) and getattr(n.func, "id", "") == "len"], "rule broken: no len()" for cmp in [n for n in ast.walk(tree) if isinstance(n, ast.Compare)]: assert all(isinstance(op, (ast.Is, ast.IsNot)) for op in cmp.ops), "rule broken: is comparisons only" print(status(None), status([]), status([0]), status(""), status("0"), status(0))

expected.text: MISSING EMPTY OK EMPTY OK EMPTY

questiontext.text:
Goal

Write four functions that show where == and is agree and where they come apart.

How this works in Python

Java taught you that == compares references and .equals compares values. Python keeps both tests and hands them to the opposite operators.

  • == is the value test. It calls the object's __eq__ method, which is Python's name for the method Java calls equals. The two underscores at each end mark a method that Python calls for you rather than one you call by name.
  • is is the identity test. It asks whether two names point at one single object in memory. That is the job Java's == does on two references.

A Java developer reaches for is as the safe general comparison and gets it exactly backwards. Worse, is often appears to work. CPython is the standard Python implementation. It keeps one cached object for every small integer from -5 to 256, and it hands out that same object every time. While it compiles the file, it also stores one shared copy of each string literal it can see. Two string literals added together are joined before the program runs. So is passes review, ships, and then fails on the value 257.

int("256") reads a string and builds an integer from it, the way Java's Integer.parseInt does. It builds that integer while the program runs, so no compiler ever sees the number.

Assignment is the other half of the lesson. alias = original copies nothing. It binds a second name to the same object. A Python variable is a name attached to an object, never a box that holds a value. Change the object through one name and the change shows through the other name, because there was only ever one list.

original = [10, 20, 30]
alias = original
alias.append(40)
print(original)          # [10, 20, 30, 40]

append adds one item to the end of a list. It changes the list in place and returns nothing.

One use of is is correct. None is a singleton, which means exactly one None object exists for the whole program. value is None is therefore both correct and the form other Python programmers expect to read.

Your task

Write four functions. None of them prints.

  • compare(left, right) returns two values, the result of left == right and the result of left is right, in that order. Separate the two with a comma to make the tuple, as the numbers topic did. This one function answers every pair below.
  • alias_demo() builds the list [10, 20, 30] and binds a second name to that same list. It appends 40 through the second name, then returns both names as original, alias.
  • tricky_pairs() returns a list of four tuples. Each tuple holds a name, a left value, and a right value, in that order. Build these four.
    • "folded literals" with "py" + "thon" on the left and "python" on the right.
    • "joined at runtime" with "".join(["py", "thon"]) on the left and "python" on the right.
    • "256 built twice" with 256 on the left and int("256") on the right.
    • "257 built twice" with 257 on the left and int("257") on the right.
  • is_missing(value) returns True when value is None.

All four pairs are equal under ==. Only two of the four are one object under is, and those two match by accident, because CPython happened to share an object. Depend on that accident and your code breaks on the value 257 or on any string built while the program runs. That gap is the whole question.

You pass when the printed output matches the expected text exactly.

Rules
  • Use is exactly twice in the whole answer. One of the two must be is None.
  • Answer every value question with ==. Do not call id(), and do not import anything.
  • Do not copy or slice the list in alias_demo. The aliasing is the entire point.
  • One implementation handles all four pairs. Special-casing any of them is cheating.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

AI allowed, on three conditions. Write your plan before you open it. Read every suggestion and reject the ones you did not plan. Type accepted code out yourself rather than pressing Tab.

question.answer:
def compare(left, right): return left == right, left is right
def alias_demo(): original = [10, 20, 30] alias = original alias.append(40) return original, alias
def tricky_pairs(): joined = "".join(["py", "thon"]) return [ ("folded literals", "py" + "thon", "python"), ("joined at runtime", joined, "python"), ("256 built twice", 256, int("256")), ("257 built twice", 257, int("257")), ]
def is_missing(value): return value is None

testcode.text: first = [1, 2, 3] second = [1, 2, 3] print(compare(first, second)) print(compare(first, first))
original, alias = alias_demo() print(original) print(alias) print(compare(original, alias))
for name, left, right in tricky_pairs(): equal, same = compare(left, right) print(f"{name:<18} == {equal!s:<5} is {same}") print(is_missing(None), is_missing(0), is_missing(""), is_missing([]))

expected.text: folded literals == True is True joined at runtime == True is False 256 built twice == True is True 257 built twice == True is False True False False False

testcode.text: import ast, inspect answer = "".join(inspect.getsource(f) for f in (compare, alias_demo, tricky_pairs, is_missing)) tree = ast.parse(answer) ids = [n for n in ast.walk(tree) if isinstance(n, ast.Call) and getattr(n.func, "id", "") == "id"] assert not ids, "rule broken: do not call id()" assert not [n for n in ast.walk(tree) if isinstance(n, (ast.Import, ast.ImportFrom))], "rule broken: no imports" ops = [op for n in ast.walk(tree) if isinstance(n, ast.Compare) for op in n.ops] assert sum(isinstance(op, (ast.Is, ast.IsNot)) for op in ops) == 2, "rule broken: use is exactly twice" assert "is None" in answer, "rule broken: one is must be is None" assert ".copy(" not in answer and "[:]" not in answer and "list(" not in answer, "rule broken: do not copy the list" box = [7] same_box = box same_box.append(8) print(compare(box, same_box), box)
